title: Independence supplies the exponent
question: Why is the probability f to the power n, rather than just f?
recap: For n independent uniformly distributed points, the chance that all lie in a fraction f of a volume is fⁿ. Perfectly locked positions instead give f; the exponent is a statement about independence.
premises: Each point is uniformly distributed over the initial volume.
The point positions are statistically independent for the independent model.
Entropy differences are related to logarithms of relative configuration probabilities.
limitations: The locked-position example is an authored mathematical counterexample, not an established alternative theory of radiation.
Spontaneous concentration probability and constrained-state entropy are related but are not the same observable.

overview.text: For n independent uniformly distributed points, the chance that all lie in a fraction f of a volume is fⁿ. Perfectly locked positions instead give f; the exponent is a statement about independence.

full.text: Each independent point has probability f of being inside the chosen fraction. For all n to be inside, multiply n independent probabilities. Taking the logarithm makes the exponent n a coefficient.

full.spoken: The probability is f to the n; the entropy difference is Boltzmann's constant times its logarithm, or n times Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of f.

full.text: With four independent points and half the volume, the probability is 1/16. If all four positions are exactly the same uniformly distributed position, the probability is 1/2 instead. Having four labels is not enough to justify four independent factors.

The concentration from V₀ to V smaller than V₀ has a negative entropy difference. Reversing the constrained comparison reverses the sign. The independent-configurations laboratory makes the probability and entropy readouts separate.

full.returnCaption: Return to the independence assumption behind the volume exponent.

items: Choose the subvolume fraction \(f = V/V_0\) between zero and one.
For a single uniform point, the probability of being inside is f.
Multiply only when the \(n\) positions are independent: \(W = f^n\).
For \(n = 4\) and \(f = 1/2\), count one all-inside result among sixteen equally likely inside/outside patterns.
Take \(\ln W = n \ln f\) and multiply by \(k_B\) for the entropy difference.
Now lock all positions to one uniform coordinate: there is only one independent condition, so \(W = f\).

margin.text: This is Boltzmann’s principle read backwards. Einstein computes how the entropy of dilute radiation changes with volume, compares it with the entropy of \(n\) independent points, \(k\ln W\) with \(W = f^n\), and concludes that such radiation behaves thermodynamically as if it consisted of \(n\) independent energy quanta. For large \(n\), \(f^n\) is astronomically small, so the laboratory reports its logarithm.
